name: Non-recovering Obstetric Brachial Plexus Lesion

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Obstetric Brachial Plexus Lesion Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Persistent upper limb paralysis or paresis beyond 3 months of age
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies confirming brachial plexus injury
MRI or ultrasound evidence of brachial plexus root avulsion or nerve disruption
Lack of functional recovery or improvement after 3-6 months post-injury
History of difficult delivery with risk factors such as shoulder dystocia or macrosomia

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Persistent paralysis beyond 3 months with electrodiagnostic confirmation and lack of functional recovery
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Early diagnosis is critical for management decisions including surgical intervention.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Flaccid paralysis of the affected upper limb
pathognomonic.notes: Typically involves shoulder, elbow, and wrist muscles
searchTerms: loss of muscle tone in arm

pathognomonic.symptomName: Loss of active shoulder abduction and external rotation
searchTerms: unable to lift or rotate shoulder

pathognomonic.symptomName: Absent biceps reflex on the affected side

common.symptomName: Muscle atrophy of the affected limb
searchTerms: shrinking muscles in affected arm or leg

common.symptomName: Sensory loss or hypoesthesia in the lateral aspect of the forearm
Wrist drop due to radial nerve involvement
common.notes: Indicates lower trunk or extended plexus injury
searchTerms: wrist drop due to nerve damage
hand weakness causing wrist to hang

common.notes: Due to long thoracic nerve palsy

occasional.symptomName: Pain or discomfort in the affected limb
occasional.notes: Neuropathic pain may develop in chronic cases
searchTerms: aching in affected arm or leg

occasional.symptomName: Joint contractures in the affected limb
occasional.notes: Secondary to muscle imbalance and immobility

occasional.symptomName: Cold intolerance of the affected hand
Delayed motor milestones related to affected limb

rare.notes: Indicates involvement of T1 sympathetic fibers
searchTerms: drooping eyelid, small pupil, and lack of sweating
Horner's syndrome signs including ptosis and miosis
eye and facial symptoms from nerve damage

rare.symptomName: Bony deformities such as glenohumeral dysplasia
rare.notes: Develops over time due to muscle imbalance

rare.symptomName: Chronic edema of the affected limb

laboratory: Electromyography showing denervation potentials and reduced motor unit recruitment
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating decreased amplitude or conduction block
imaging: MRI showing nerve root avulsion or pseudomeningocele formation
Ultrasound demonstrating nerve discontinuity or neuroma
other: Clinical observation of limb posture and muscle tone
Functional assessment of limb movement and reflexes

distinguishingFeatures: Usually involves upper trunk only without root avulsion
Absence of persistent paralysis beyond 3 months
Presents with hand and wrist weakness rather than shoulder
May be associated with Horner syndrome more frequently
Progressive symptoms rather than congenital onset
Imaging shows mass lesion rather than nerve disruption

redFlags: Absence of spontaneous motor recovery by 3 months of age
Presence of Horner syndrome indicating root avulsion
Severe muscle atrophy and joint contractures developing early
references: Narakas AO. Obstetrical brachial plexus injuries. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1987;(222):43-52.
Pondaag W, Malessy MJ. The natural history of obstetric brachial plexus palsy: a systematic review. Dev Med Child Neurol. 2014;56(7):629-634.
Gilbert A. Obstetrical brachial plexus injuries. J Hand Surg Am. 1999;24(4):786-792.
